Issued at 1152 AM MDT Sat Oct 10 2026

DEEP MOISTURE INCREASES THIS WEEKEND:

Scattered showers are tracking across the area this morning with
some isolated thunderstorm activity although rain rates remain
light with gusty outflow winds underneath these showers.
Tropical Storm Rachel is currently off the Baja coast and is
anticipated to track inland across SoCal through western Arizona
and into western Utah by Sunday. Deeper moisture from the
remnants of this tropical system is expected to move across the
area from the southwest this evening and overnight into Sunday
with more widespread showers and embedded thunderstorms. This
moisture is being pulled into a low pressure trough over the
Pacific Northwest that will dive southward and deepen over the
Great Basin, with a robust jet setting up across Utah. PWAT 
anomalies are expected to climb above 250 percent of normal this
evening and peak near 300 percent of normal through Sunday. The
details remain a challenge with the forecast as given this 
abundant moisture this evening and overnight, we could see more 
cloud cover which could inhibit convective potential and result 
in more of a steady light to moderate rainfall overnight into 
Sunday morning. 

STRONG TO SEVERE STORMS POSSIBLE SUNDAY:

How much clearing occurs Sunday morning and afternoon remains 
to be seen but models are hinting at a bit of a dry slot working
in across the Four Corners which could result in some areas of 
clearing and more sunshine to act on the deep moisture and 
instability in place. If this happens, more robust convection 
looks possible, especially across eastern Utah and far western 
Colorado. Given the proximity of the low from the remnants of 
Tropical Storm Rachel, strong gradient winds are expected as 
well as stronger shear upwards of 40 to 50 kts. CAPE is fairly 
modest around 500 J/kg across southeast Utah especially, so with
more sunshine, we could see stronger storms develop Sunday 
afternoon and evening along this moisture gradient. Some could 
potentially be severe as well and it appears like the primary 
threat would be outflow winds. Hail is still possible as well 
given the shear but it looks like more speed shear than 
directional which would tend to result in more of a strong wind 
threat. With the deep moisture in place, any storms would be 
capable of locally heavier rainfall rates, which would cause 
concern for flash flooding but it's hard to pinpoint exactly 
where this threat is the greatest and it will be dependent on 
storm mode. All in all, the eastern Uintas are still forecasted 
to see the higher rainfall totals of 1 to 3 inches through 
Monday morning with the San Juans and Abajos seeing over an inch
of rainfall but this may be more gradual over the course of the
next 48 hours. Localized flash flooding is possible though with
any stronger convection but storm motion will be fairly swift. 
Given those factors, confidence remains too low at this time for
a flood watch.

STRONG WINDS EXPECTED SUNDAY:

In addition to the storm potential, the gradient winds increase
with better mixing possible Sunday afternoon and evening if this
clearing pans out. Forecasted winds across southeast Utah and
portions of southwest Colorado are already expected to gust 40
to 50 mph, so issued a Wind Advisory from 9 am Sunday through
midnight Sunday night for those areas. Convection would enhance
those gusts where some locally higher gusts exceeding 55 mph are
possible if stronger convection develops. 

LOOKING AHEAD NEXT WEEK:

Things will taper off a bit on Monday as moisture decreases and
instability decreases but a 100 kt jet remains in place so
breezy conditions and decent shear could lead to some stronger
storms still possible during the afternoon. The next system to
impact the region is an early season winter storm as the cold- 
core Pacific Northwest low drops down through the Great Basin 
before lifting to the northeast across the region Tuesday 
evening and Wednesday. This won't bring a lot of snow to the 
region, but we will likely see some winter driving conditions on
the mountain passes with low visibilities and periods of slick 
roads. We will likely see snow down to 8,000 ft, but don't 
expect any accumulation below about 10,000 ft. Stay tuned for 
updates on this one too.
